claims.text: The investigated material is an as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy thin coating on a conventional metal substrate.
The baseline coating has not received an engineered pre-oxidation treatment.
Annealing under controlled oxygen partial pressure can form a thin oxide scale on the coating.
The pre-oxidation treatment can produce a uniform, continuous oxide scale.
The engineered scale may contain spinel and chromium- or iron-based oxides.
Oxide scales formed at elevated temperature can remain adherent to the underlying alloy.
The relevant sliding regime is approximately 400–600 °C.
Thermal activation in the proposed regime promotes oxidation.
Thermal activation in the proposed regime produces significant dislocation activity.
The oxide layer acts as a barrier to dislocation motion.
The oxide layer mitigates oxidation-driven surface softening.
The oxide layer limits the initiation and propagation of dislocation slip and microscopic plastic deformation during sliding.
Pre-oxidized coatings will have a lower specific wear rate than as-deposited coatings during high-temperature sliding.
Pre-oxidized coatings will show less localized plastic deformation than as-deposited coatings during high-temperature sliding.
The predicted benefit requires the oxide scale to remain stable and continuous.
An oxide scale that is too thick, discontinuous, or brittle may crack and eliminate the predicted benefit.
The optimal oxide thickness, composition, and adhesion are not yet defined.

contradictions.description: The boundary restricts the hypothesis to cases where the oxide remains stable and continuous and says cracking may place the result outside the expected regime, whereas the falsification rule treats cracking or delamination without benefit as a falsifying outcome. A failed mediator should be distinguished from a test of the mechanism under its stated boundary conditions.
